newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: Ireland sees EBR undershoot of 300mln punts-finmin.
newsitem.headline: Ireland sees EBR undershoot of 300mln punts-finmin.

text.p: Ireland's Department of Finance said on Wednesday that it expected to undershoot the 1996 target Exchequer Borrowing Requirement (EBR) by around 300 million punts.
Finance minister Ruairi Quinn, in an annual budget last February, set a target EBR of 729 million punts.

"It's difficult at this stage to predict exactly where we'll be, but we're certainly expecting to be 300 million or more below the budget estimate," said Michael Tutty, second secretary at the Department of Finance.

"We're talking about being down to (an end-year EBR of) 450 million, and perhaps even down to 350 million. Somewhere in that range is where we expect to be," he told a news conference on the release of Ireland's third quarter EBR.

Third quarter EBR figures showed a surplus of 185 million punts, the first time in more than 30 years that a third-quarter surplus has been recorded. But Tutty said timing factors had boosted the surplus and the underlying position was not so strong.

Tutty said tax revenue would be around 300 million punts above target at end-1996, while non-tax revenue would be around 50 million above target. Supply services expenditure would exceed the budget target by around 100 million punts, he said.
Taking into account other minor factors, the overall EBR undershoot would therefore be around 300 million, Tutty said.
The expected 300-million-punt tax receipts overshoot was divided fairly equally between income tax, corporation tax and indirect taxes, Tutty said.

"Almost all of the tax levels are ahead of budget estimates and that certainly reflects higher economic activity (and) retail sales. The income tax returns suggest there was much stronger employment growth than we had predicted," Tutty said.
"So we're expecting to be at least 300 million ahead of the budget estimate for tax revenue," he said.
The expected overshoot of 50 million in non-tax revenue was entirely due to an unexpected reimbursement from the EU.
"This once-off gain had not been anticipated in the budget arithmetic and will bring the outturn for non-tax revenue ahead of target," Tutty said.

Unanticipated expenditure due to the mad cow disease crisis, higher-than-expected agricultural fines and a new package of crime measures would push supply services expenditure to around 100 million punts above target, he said.
The NTMA's debt service outturn for 1996 would probably be around 50 million punts below the budget estimate, Tutty added.
